Summary: The paper builds a benchmark for writing OMIM phenotype entries from exactly the papers the curators cited (100 entries, 2-12 references each, 515 papers of which 19% are open-access full text; causal gene withheld) and compares generation strategies with the model (Claude Opus 5.5), guards, claim-level audit and scoring held fixed. Strategies span read-and-write (direct reading in one prompt; an agentic curator with read/search tools), extract-then-write (an evidence graph; a per-patient case table), memory-first (recall then verify), a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand passages, a reconciled case database, a learned curation guide). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', scores what a draft says about each cited paper against fixed fact lists split once from OMIM's allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts). Headline results: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage of their facts from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries, Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a); reading strategies convey 91-94% of facts the supplied text is judged to state and under 7% of facts it does not (Fig. 2c, Table 18); the agent and evidence graph are not distinguishable from direct reading, the case-table implementation trails by 1.9 points (Table 1); a per-paper completeness pass adds 2.6 points on 38 held-out entries without lowering judged support (Sec. 4.3); exploratory runs of PaperQA2 and GraphRAG convey fewer facts and STORM produced no output (Sec. 4.4); and planted-error tests show the audit catches single-value substitutions, citation swaps and negation deletions but cannot see added citations or omissions (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4). Every judgement (fact splitting, coverage, 'stated', audit) is made by the writer's own model family, and no human validated any of them.
Strengths: Careful experimental control: one model, one set of guards, one audit and one scoring pipeline across all strategies, with paired per-entry comparisons, percentile bootstrap intervals, exact sign tests, Holm adjustment on secondary measures, and run-to-run and judge-variation yardsticks reported separately from the inferential test (Sec. 3.3, Appendix E, Table 19).

The within-paper access manipulation (hiding the full text of the same papers and re-writing from abstracts, with and without second-hand passages; Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2a, Table 22) is a clean design that separates what the source exposes from how a strategy reads, and the 'stated / not stated' split of every fixed fact (Fig. 2b-c, Table 18) is a useful diagnostic for locating where coverage is lost.

Fixing the fact lists once, without sight of any draft, and showing that per-draft splitting inflates levels by 2-5 points (Table 5) is a sound and reusable measurement lesson; likewise the symmetric completion rule, the intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Table 10) and the candid account of an earlier analysis that had to be corrected (Appendix M.4).

The audit stress test is informative about the blind spots of claim-level citation audits: the best-verdict-over-cited-papers rule makes added irrelevant citations invisible (0/30 flagged although the added paper's own verdict was unsupported for all 176 claims), omissions are invisible by construction, and recovered per-paper verdicts show 4-7% unsupported (claim, cited paper) pairs in real multi-citation paragraphs (Sec. 4.5, Fig. 4, Tables 47-50).

Claims are scoped with unusual care: null results are not presented as equivalence (Sec. 4.2), exploratory analyses with 4-10 entries are labelled as such, the case-table deficit is attributed to 'our implementation', and a matched ablation (Appendix F, Tables 20-21) shows how much implementation settings move the extract-then-write strategies.

The reading-better experiment (Sec. 4.3, Appendix I) was designed after the main study, frozen on three training entries and run on held-out entries, and its gain is localised to facts the text states (Fig. 3b), with fidelity checked on an audited subsample (Table 30).
Weaknesses: The entire measurement chain is unvalidated by humans and judged by the writer's own model family: fact splitting, the present/partly/absent/contradicted coverage judgement, the 'stated in the supplied text' judgement on which the central access argument rests (Sec. 4.1), and the audit itself (Sec. 3.3, Limitation (i)). Judge-variation results (Table 19) show self-consistency, not validity, and the related work cited by the paper (Panickssery et al., 2024; Shankar et al., 2024) is exactly why this matters. Even a small expert-annotated sample of fact splits and coverage judgements, or a cross-family judge on the 30-entry replicate subset, would substantially strengthen every headline number.

The 'stated' and 'conveyed' judgements are made by the same model family on correlated inputs, so the 91-94% ceiling on stated facts and the under-7% rate on not-stated facts (Fig. 2c, Table 18) may partly reflect shared judgement tendencies rather than the true information content of the text. The paper notes this caveat (Sec. 4.1) but it bears directly on the main conclusion that access, not strategy, bounds agreement.

The regime tested favours direct reading by design: entries have 2-12 references whose text fits one prompt (median about 39k characters, Sec. 4.4), and the reading strategies are near ceiling on stated facts. The settings where intermediate representations and agents are expected to help (many relevant papers, long inputs) could not be compared: the large-entry experiment yielded 0 comparable entries because of safety-filter stops (Sec. 4.4, Appendix K.2), and padding used unrelated papers that no draft cited. The near-null strategy comparison therefore has limited generality, and the 'access bounds agreement' finding is, as the paper itself says, expected (Sec. 1).

The reference is narrow and indirect. Only OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs are scored; narrative sections are not public (Sec. 3.1). About 68% of fixed facts concern abstract-only papers and 43% are not stated in the supplied text (Table 18), so much of the primary endpoint's denominator is unreachable by any reading strategy, compressing the room for strategies to differ. Only about 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference (Appendix H), so most generated content is evaluated only by the unvalidated same-family audit.

Strategy-level conclusions are sensitive to implementation and entry selection. The case-table deficit (-1.9, CI -3.1 to -0.8) does not survive the sign test (p = 0.071) or the intention-to-treat analysis (-1.4, -4.2 to +1.4; Table 10), and largely disappears when extraction effort and synopsis assignment are matched (+2.1 step, Appendix F). The evidence graph moves from -0.5 on the 93 entries to +1.0 on the 38 ablation entries and +1.8 when matched, with sign reversals across entry groups (Sec. 4.2, Appendix F). The main strategies were also developed on the entries they are evaluated on (Limitation (vi)). This makes it hard to draw paradigm-level conclusions rather than statements about these particular implementations.

Single model, single run per entry, no temperature or seed control, and entries lost unevenly to safety-filter stops whose reasons are not visible (Sec. 3.2, Table 4). The 93-entry comparison set is thus selected by the model's filter, and the 2026 post-creation-date check retains only 20 of 30 entries (Appendix M.2). No second model family is tested as writer, so it is unknown whether the ranking or the near-null differences transfer.

The released-pipeline comparison (Sec. 4.4, Appendix J) is too weak to support even the hedged conclusion that 'our implementations are not outperformed': PaperQA2 ran without its agent, GraphRAG on 4 entries with one small local embedding model, both QA systems answered six fixed section questions rather than the task they were designed for, only the authors' drafts were repaired, and STORM produced no output. This section adds length without adding reliable evidence.

Benchmark reusability is unclear. The ethics statement says curator text is not redistributed and released score files carry fact identifiers and statuses, not wording. If the fixed fact lists themselves are not released, a new strategy cannot be scored against the same denominators without re-splitting, which the paper shows shifts levels by 2-5 points (Table 5). This weakens contribution (1).

Recall-then-verify is constrained to add nothing from the papers, so its low coverage (14.6%) is largely by construction (Sec. 4.2); presenting it as one of three paradigms inflates the apparent breadth of the comparison without testing whether verification after recall can help.

Presentation is very dense for an ICLR main-track paper. The main text compresses roughly a dozen experiments (main comparison, hidden full text, second-hand passages, ablation, contamination, two add-ons, four reading-better arms, three released pipelines, padding, large entries, seven planted-error classes) into ten pages with heavy hedging and many inline intervals, and 52 appendix tables. Key definitions (e.g., how facts are split, what 'partly present' means operationally, how the six section questions were posed to released systems) are hard to find, and the core contribution is difficult to extract on a first read. The title's question is answered in a way readers may find unsurprising.
Questions: Can you provide any human validation of the measurement chain: for example, a domain expert annotating a random sample of a few hundred (fact, draft) pairs for present/partly/absent, a sample of fact splits for faithfulness to the curator paragraph, and a sample of 'stated in the supplied text' judgements? Agreement with the model judge on these would directly support Figs. 2-3 and Table 1.

Could you re-score the 30-entry replicate subset with a judge from a different model family, and ideally run direct reading and the evidence graph with a writer from another family, to estimate self-preference bias and whether the near-null strategy differences transfer?

Will the fixed fact lists (the text of each fact, not only identifiers) be released or deterministically reconstructable from public data, so that a new strategy can be scored against exactly the same 6,652 facts? If reconstruction requires re-splitting with the model, how stable are the resulting lists?

What kinds of facts account for the case table's -8.4-point deficit on stated full-text facts (e.g., functional assays, population or segregation data that are not per-patient records)? A breakdown by fact type would show whether the deficit is a property of the representation or of the extraction schema.

Are safety-filter stops associated with entry content (particular phenotypes, ages, or types of clinical description)? If so, how does this selection affect the 93-entry comparison set and the large-entry experiment?

How was 'partly present' operationalised in the coverage judgement, and how do the main differences change under full-credit-only scoring for each restriction in Table 18 (the 'fully' row in Table 5 is given only for all facts)?

For the access experiment, how much of the 36.1% abstract-only coverage is attributable to memory? The creation-band decline in abstract-only coverage (49.8% to 37.9%, Sec. 4.2) suggests memorisation contributes; could the hidden-full-text comparison be reported separately for the 2026 entries or the newest band?

Is there a setting with many relevant papers (e.g., large entries scored only on the subset of references covered by curator paragraphs, or entries assembled from relevant but uncited papers) where the strategies could be compared despite the stops, given that this is where the paper's own discussion expects designs to separate?
Limitations: One model family wrote, extracted, audited and judged everything, with no human validation of any judgement (acknowledged, Limitation (i)).

Reference covers only OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs plus HPO, gene and inheritance tables; only about 24% of draft statements have a counterpart, so most generated content is checked only by the audit (Limitation (ii), Appendix H).
Entries are small (2-12 references, fit one prompt) and selected for being well annotated; large sets of relevant papers were not compared (Limitation (viii), Sec. 4.4).
Every strategy receives the curators' reference list; literature finding was tested on ten entries only (Limitation (iii), Appendix M.3).
Only openly licensed full text without supplements was used; papers free to read but not openly licensed, about a third of curator facts, were not tested (Limitation (iv), Sec. 4.3).
Strategies were developed on the evaluation entries; safety-filter stops remove entries unevenly; no temperature or seed control (Limitations (vi)-(vii)).

The audit checks fidelity to the cited text, not correctness, and is blind to over-citation and omissions (Limitation (ix), Sec. 4.5). The paper discusses these limitations thoroughly; the missing piece is any attempt to mitigate the first one with even a small human or cross-family validation.
